response.title: Why patients return to hospital from hospital at home
response.subtitle: Design not yet settled: the request asks why, not how often
response.statement: Patients treated in the hospital-at-home program appear to be readmitted more often than ward patients (17 against 12 percent at 30 days on the program dashboard), most visibly those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure. The program does not know why patients return, whether returns follow clinical worsening, falls, carer strain or night-time gaps, or which returns could be avoided. Managers want the answer before adding beds.
response.whoAffected: Patients admitted to hospital at home (412 in the last year), their family carers, the program's nurses and physicians, and the managers deciding on expansion.
response.whatHurts: A readmission undoes the purpose of care at home, exposes frail patients to a hospital stay they hoped to avoid and can leave carers feeling they failed.
response.currentPractice: Readmissions are counted on a dashboard; their reasons and the patient and carer experience before the return are not recorded.
response.whyNow: An expansion decision next year and a dashboard figure that worries managers.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients who choose hospital at home stay at home safely when they can, and return to hospital only when hospital care is what they need.
response.summary: Problem framed around the unexplained readmissions; the design is left unresolved because the request does not say whether the aim is to measure, compare or explain.

records.title: Hospital-at-home versus ward care for acute medical admissions: 30-day readmission in a matched cohort
records.authors: Okafor-Lindqvist A, Brandt-Mensah J, Ruiz-Halvorsen P
records.venue: Journal of Acute Care at Home
records.abstract: We matched 1,860 patients admitted to a hospital-at-home service with 1,860 ward patients by diagnosis, age and frailty score. Thirty-day readmission was 15.8 percent after hospital at home and 13.1 percent after ward care; after adjustment, the difference was not clear (adjusted odds ratio 1.12, 95 percent CI 0.94 to 1.34). Readmission was higher after hospital at home for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and similar for other conditions. Patients who lived alone were more often readmitted in both groups. The study could not say why patients returned or whether returns were avoidable.

records.title: Carers' experiences of acute care at home: responsibility, uncertainty and the decision to call
records.abstract: We spoke with 22 family carers of patients treated in a hospital-at-home service. Carers described taking on monitoring they did not feel trained for, especially at night, and uncertainty about when to call the team rather than an ambulance. Several described calling an ambulance because the service's night line felt slow or because they did not want to disturb the team. Carers who had a written plan for night-time worsening described fewer emergency calls. Carers with their own health problems or other caring duties described the most strain.

records.title: Hospital at home for acute medical conditions: a systematic review of readmission and mortality
records.authors: Petrov-Oduya S, Castellanos-Reid D, Mbeki-Holt K, Nakamura-Adu F
records.abstract: We included 16 randomised trials and 21 observational studies of hospital at home for acute medical conditions. In trials, readmission within 90 days was similar to ward care (risk ratio 1.05, 95 percent CI 0.88 to 1.25) and mortality did not differ. Observational studies reported more variable readmission, with higher rates in services that took older and frailer patients. Few studies reported the reasons for readmission or the views of patients and carers. The trial populations were selected and may not reflect services that accept most referrals.

records.title: Deciding to transfer back: clinicians' escalation decisions in hospital-at-home services
records.abstract: We held semi-structured conversations with 18 nurses and physicians working in three hospital-at-home services about decisions to transfer patients back to hospital. Clinicians described lower thresholds for transfer at night, when fewer staff were available to visit, and when they did not know the patient. Handovers between day and night teams often lacked a shared plan for worsening. Several described transfers that could have been avoided with a visit within two hours. Services with a named senior clinician on call described fewer night transfers.

records.title: Reasons for readmission after hospital at home: a structured review of 300 readmissions
records.authors: Achterberg-Ng R, Delacroix-Mwangi E, Fischer-Adeyemi O
records.venue: Journal of Acute Care at Home
records.abstract: Two clinicians independently reviewed 300 consecutive readmissions within 30 days of discharge from a hospital-at-home service. The readmission was for the same condition in 41 percent, a fall in 22 percent, carer breakdown or social crisis in 18 percent and a new condition in the rest. Reviewers judged 34 percent of readmissions potentially avoidable, most often those after carer breakdown or night-time worsening. Agreement between reviewers on avoidability was moderate (kappa 0.58). Records rarely documented what patients and carers had understood about when to seek help.

records.title: Information power and sample size in qualitative studies of care transitions
records.abstract: We reviewed 64 qualitative studies of care transitions and the sample sizes they justified. Studies with a narrow aim, participants with specific experience of the transition and a strong analytic dialogue reported adequate information with 12 to 20 interviews per participant group. Studies that mixed patients, carers and clinicians in one sample needed larger totals to say anything about each group. We recommend stating the aim, the specificity of the sample and the analysis strategy before recruitment and revisiting the target during analysis rather than citing saturation alone.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Readmission after hospital at home is similar to ward care in trials and not clearly different after matching in one cohort, so the local dashboard gap may partly reflect who is admitted. What the evidence does not explain is why patients return: carers describe night-time uncertainty and slow night lines, clinicians describe lower thresholds for transfer at night and weak handover plans, and a record review attributes a fifth of readmissions to carer breakdown and a third to potentially avoidable causes. These findings point to an explanatory question that interviews with patients, carers and clinicians can answer.
response.gradeRationale: Observational and small qualitative studies from single services, one systematic review of selected trials; consistent themes but indirect for this program.
response.summary: Six records appraised; five source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

response.reading: A readmission from hospital at home is the end of a sequence of decisions made at home: the patient's worsening, the carer's judgement about whom to call, the night line's response and the clinician's threshold for transfer. The evidence shows each of these links exists elsewhere but not how they combine in this program. Case mix may explain part of the dashboard gap. The people who can explain the sequence are the patients who returned, their carers and the clinicians who decided.

store.title: Why patients return to hospital from hospital at home

response.overview: Qualitative interview study of readmissions within 30 days of hospital-at-home care, with three participant groups (patients, carers, clinicians) sampled around recent readmissions.
response.population: Patients readmitted within 30 days of discharge from the program in the study period (target 16), their family carers (target 10) and program nurses and physicians involved in the episode (target 10); purposive sampling for diagnosis (COPD, heart failure, other), living alone, time of worsening and language.
response.exposure: Readmission within 30 days after hospital-at-home care (the phenomenon of interest).
response.procedures: Eligible readmissions are identified weekly from the dashboard. A research nurse not involved in the patient's care invites the patient and carer within four weeks of the readmission; interviews last about 45 minutes at home, by phone or in hospital, with interpreters where needed. Clinician interviews follow the same episodes. A short structured summary of each episode is drawn from the record to anchor the interviews. Interviews are recorded, transcribed and analysed with reflexive thematic analysis by two analysts, one with nursing and one with patient-partner background.

response.summary: Interview study of about 36 participants in three groups around recent readmissions.

response.designSummary: Qualitative interview study; no statistical testing.
response.sampleSize: Targets of 16 patients, 10 carers and 10 clinicians follow the retrieved guidance of 12 to 20 interviews per group for a narrow aim with a specific sample (c5); carers and clinicians have lower targets because their accounts are anchored to the same episodes. The targets are revisited during analysis, and recruitment stops for a group when new interviews add no new account of the pathway.
response.primaryAnalysis: Reflexive thematic analysis by two analysts, coding each group separately and then comparing accounts of the same episodes across patient, carer and clinician.
response.secondaryAnalysis: A short descriptive table of the episodes (diagnosis, time of worsening, who called, route back) from the record summaries, without inferential statistics.

response.risks: Low physical risk; emotional distress when recounting a readmission, and concern among clinicians about blame.
response.consent: Written or recorded verbal consent by a research nurse not involved in care, after at least 24 hours to consider; patients who lack capacity are not interviewed, but their carers may be; clinicians consent separately and may withdraw their interview.
response.data: Recordings deleted after transcription check; transcripts de-identified; quotes reported without role details that could identify a clinician in a small team.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients living alone, with limited English, with low income or with cognitive impairment, and carers with their own health problems are the least likely to volunteer and the most likely to be readmitted. Sampling targets them deliberately, interpreters and phone interviews are offered, and carers are offered a small voucher from existing patient-partner funds.
response.effectiveness: The study succeeds if it identifies changes the program can make before expansion.
response.efficiency: About 36 interviews within existing staff time.
response.costs: Transcription through the hospital's approved service; vouchers from patient-partner funds.
response.grants: None needed; a later evaluation of changes could seek funding.
response.partnerships: Two patient partners with hospital-at-home experience and one carer partner review the interview guides and the themes.

response.title: Why patients return to hospital from hospital at home: a qualitative study with patients, carers and clinicians
response.abstract: Aim: to explain how readmissions within 30 days of hospital-at-home care come about. Design: qualitative interviews with patients, family carers and clinicians anchored to recent readmissions, analysed with reflexive thematic analysis. Results and conclusions will be written after analysis.
response.introduction: Hospital at home achieves readmission rates similar to ward care in trials, but local services see returns they cannot explain. Few studies report the views of patients and carers about how a readmission came about.
response.methods: About 36 participants in three groups (patients, carers, clinicians) were sampled purposively around recent readmissions and interviewed within four weeks, with record summaries to anchor their accounts. Two analysts with different backgrounds used reflexive thematic analysis.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present themes by participant group and the accounts of shared episodes.
response.discussion: The discussion will relate the themes to night-time escalation, carer strain and handover, and compare accounts of the same episodes across groups. It will state which changes the program could test before adding beds.
response.limitations: The study covers one program, and accounts given after a readmission are subject to recall. Clinicians may be reluctant to describe their own decisions.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis. It will offer explanations and candidate changes, not rates.
